sketches.title: Spin Cycle
sketches.premise: Two laundrette disasters fight by making each other’s mess worse in a way that also fixes it. Put down one machine, substance, or laundry problem that acts on the thing before it. The last move that cannot cleanly transform the standing mess loses.
sketches.criterion: The Judge checks whether your thing directly changes the standing thing into a cleaner, sorted, dried, pressed, or otherwise laundered state; merely avoiding it, surviving it, making a bigger version of it, or naming a nearby laundry item does not count.
sketches.move_shape: Say: “I am [thing], and I [direct action] the standing thing.” Example: “I am detergent, and I dissolve the grease in that oil stain.”
sketches.first_card: I am a red sock, and I bleed dye into the white shirt.

sketches.title: Lost Property
sketches.premise: Two players run the launderette’s lost-property counter. Each turn, name one ordinary object that can plainly claim, replace, contain, reveal, or return the object just put down. If your object only sits beside it or happens to be found in the same place, the desk clerk sends it back.
sketches.criterion: The Judge checks whether the new object has a direct, recognizable way to take custody of, identify, replace, contain, or return the standing object; dodging, hiding, merely surviving, a larger copy, and a cousin from the same object family all fail.
sketches.move_shape: Say: “I am [object], and I [specific recovery action] the standing object.” Example: “I am a label, and I identify the coat nobody claimed.”
sketches.first_card: I am a single sock, abandoned under the folding table.

sketches.title: Change Machine
sketches.premise: The launderette’s change machine is malfunctioning, and every player feeds it a thing that directly converts the thing before it into something usable. The machine accepts physical changes, money changes, and plain wordplay only when the new thing is the mechanism, not a decorative pun.
sketches.criterion: The Judge checks whether your standing thing directly changes, breaks down, exchanges, or makes usable what came before; merely sidestepping it, enduring it, making a bigger version, or offering a same-family cousin does not beat it.
sketches.move_shape: Say: “I am [thing], and I turn the standing thing into [result] by [mechanism].” Example: “I am a coin slot, and I turn the loose coin into a paid wash.”
sketches.first_card: I am a crumpled five-pound note, useless to the coin machine.

sketches.title: Fold or Fail
sketches.premise: Two players fold laundry into increasingly specific shapes, tools, and traps. Your folded form must physically or plainly use the standing form, not merely resemble it; if it only avoids the old shape, the pile stays on the floor and your turn is toast.
sketches.criterion: The Judge checks whether the new folded thing directly encloses, cuts, supports, traps, hides, or transforms the standing thing; dodging, surviving, a bigger version, and a related garment from the same family do not count.
sketches.move_shape: Say: “I fold into [thing], and I use it to [direct action] the standing thing.” Example: “I fold into a pouch, and I contain the loose buttons.”
sketches.first_card: I am a flat towel spread across the folding table.

sketches.title: Spin the Drum
sketches.premise: The washing-machine drum is a tiny universe. Each turn names one thing that the spinning wash plainly does to the thing before it: strips it, tangles it, separates it, breaks it, or changes its state. The host reports the result with the warmth of a man watching a sock die.
sketches.criterion: The Judge checks for a direct washing-machine action or consequence that overcomes the standing thing; merely escaping the drum, lasting longer, using a bigger copy, or naming a related laundry object is a loss.
sketches.move_shape: Say: “I am [thing in the drum], and the spin [directly does something] to the standing thing.” Example: “I am a zipper, and I snag the loose lace until it knots.”
sketches.first_card: I am a loose lace, floating harmlessly in the wash.

sketches.title: Stain Court
sketches.premise: A laundrette judge hears cases between stains and their punishments. One player names a standing stain or laundry mark; the other answers with a plain household thing that directly removes, covers, tests, or proves what that mark is. A vague insult is not evidence, though it may still be funny.
sketches.criterion: The Judge checks whether the answer directly acts on the standing mark to remove it, cover it, identify it, or establish its cause; avoiding the mark, surviving it, making a stronger-looking mark, or naming a similar stain loses.
sketches.move_shape: Say: “I am [household thing], and I [direct action] the standing stain.” Example: “I am vinegar, and I break the smell of sweat in the armpit.”
sketches.first_card: I am a lipstick stain on a white collar.
